description: Routing decisions: pharmacist-led care for low-to-moderate complexity, telemedicine specialist co-management, and automated scheduling for high-urgency physician needs.

samples.user: A 35-year-old with no significant history reports a localised, painful red sore at the corner of the mouth and a cold sore on the lip that started yesterday, otherwise well. Where should this be routed: pharmacist, physician appointment, or ED? Justify.

A 7-month-old infant has a high fever, is floppy and difficult to rouse, is not feeding, and has a non-blanching rash. Determine the routing destination and the scheduling/escalation action the system should take.

A patient with HIV on stable antiretroviral therapy needs to start a statin for high cholesterol and is worried about interactions. Describe how a clinic pharmacist and a remote HIV specialist should co-manage this via telemedicine.

A 55-year-old reports unintentional weight loss of about 6 kg over 3 months, a persistent change in bowel habit, and occasional blood in the stool, currently feeling otherwise well. Where should this be routed and why is pharmacist-only care unsafe?

A healthy 22-year-old has mild, painless threadworm symptoms (perianal itching, worse at night) confirmed by seeing small white worms, no other symptoms. Is this suitable for pharmacist-led care, and what would that involve?

A patient with type 2 diabetes asks the pharmacist a routine question about switching to a once-weekly GLP-1 device, but also mentions a foot blister that has turned into a deep, non-healing ulcer over 2 weeks with surrounding redness. Describe how to split the routing between pharmacist-led care and physician escalation.
